To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

information about the neural representation of a visual stimulus can be extracted from patterns of voxel responses in early visual cortex more than one second before the average response of that region deviates from baseline.

(1) stimulus information is detectable in the hemodynamic signal before the peak of regional hemodynamic response; (2) the peak of classification accuracy precedes the peak of regional response; (3) both effects are strongest in early visual cortex; (4) these effects are not observed in higher level visual areas; (5) the peak of hemodynamic response is delayed in higher level areas; and (6) the peak of the hemodynamic response is more variable across subjects in higher level

pattern classification can detect information about the neural activity in a region before the average response to a stimulus has deviated from baseline and that classification accuracy peaks before average regional hemodynamic activity peaks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the brain processes visual information and the temporal dynamics of the hemodynamic response.
understanding the temporal dynamics of neural activity, and how this activity can be detected in hemodynamic responses measured using fMRI.
the relationship between the hemodynamic response and the neural activity that generates it.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the temporal relationship between the average hemodynamic signal and the MVPA classification signal is region-dependent and the classification signal precedes the hemodynamic response in primary visual areas.
pattern classification of fMRI signals in early visual cortex precedes region-average responses by several seconds.

the hemodynamic response in primary visual cortex can be detected in a pattern classification analysis more than a second prior to the average hemodynamic signal reaching a statistically significant level, and that this effect is restricted to primary visual cortex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hemodynamic response in V1 is a poor proxy for the neural response to visual stimuli, and this is true even in the absence of any explicit task.
the hemodynamic response is a poor proxy for the neural response, and that the hemodynamic signal should not be interpreted as an average of the neural response.
MVPA is sensitive enough to detect the early stages of the hemodynamic response in V1, and that this response can be used to classify visual stimuli.
The main takeaway from our work is that
information about the neural activity in early visual cortex can be detected in fMRI signals more than a second earlier than the average hemodynamic signal reaches its peak.
the temporal evolution of the hemodynamic response in V1 can be used as a marker to predict when the pattern classification accuracy is at a maximum.
MVPA can be used in combination with high temporal resolution fMRI to investigate the temporal dynamics of information processing in the brain.
